assessment.nobel_worthiness: Random-coefficients discrete-choice demand estimation with endogenous prices (BLP) and the dynamic oligopoly framework (Ericson-Pakes) turned empirical industrial organisation into a quantitative discipline. They underpin merger analysis, antitrust practice, auctions and trade, so the methods have been used far beyond their origin.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the clear core for demand estimation, and Pakes also anchors dynamic industry models and estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin made important parallel or follow-on contributions. The three-name limit excludes them, so the choice of three involves a judgement about the core.
assessment.maturity: BLP appeared in 1995 and the dynamic-industry work in the 1990s and 2000s, so there are about three decades of confirmed use in academia, regulators and industry. The work is highly mature.
uncertainties: The three-name limit forces a choice among Bresnahan, Reiss and the other contributors.
The committee may see this as too close to the earlier IO and auction-theory prizes, or as a narrow subfield.
My own background in industrial organisation may make me overestimate its centrality; the profile discloses that field, and I apply common criteria.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz (2003) introduced firm heterogeneity and selection into trade, which shifted the field's focus from industries to firms. It explains exporter premia, the reallocation channel for gains from trade, and the use of firm-level data. Helpman's work on trade with increasing returns and heterogeneous firms provides the broader framework.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is central to the heterogeneous-firm model. Helpman is a leading architect of the new trade theory and of its firm-level extensions. Redding is also a strong contributor but is secondary to the two names proposed. Krugman (already a laureate) and Bernard, Eaton and Kortum are outside this candidate's credited names, so credit may be spread more widely than the ballot shows.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of empirical confirmation using firm-level customs and production data. The framework has been refined and tested extensively.
uncertainties: Helpman is also credited under B030, and the committee might prefer to recognise him through the trade-and-politics work.
Quantitative gains-from-trade results are sensitive to model assumptions, which affects how much the empirical record confirms the theory.
The share of credit owed to related work outside the credited names, such as Bernard-Jensen on exporter facts, is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidity, the Calvo pricing model, the Taylor rule and the Woodford-style New Keynesian framework are the dominant intellectual basis of modern central-bank analysis and inflation targeting. The practical influence on policy is very large.
assessment.attribution: Calvo supplied the pricing building block, Taylor the policy-rule and staggered-contract tradition, and Woodford the integrated microfounded framework. The ballot names eight people, and Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have also contributed substantially. A three-name selection is therefore contestable, and part of the framework's lineage lies with already-honoured laureates.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of development and extensive policy use. The 2008-2022 experience (the financial crisis, then the inflation surge) gave a mixed test of the framework.
uncertainties: Attribution is diffuse across several contributors, so the three-name set is open to dispute.
Parts of the framework have been criticised after the financial crisis and the post-2021 inflation, and heterogeneous-agent models partly challenge it.
Overlap with earlier macro prizes (Lucas, Phelps, Kydland-Prescott) makes the incremental contribution harder to define.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bayesian persuasion and information design provide a general tool for how a sender optimally shapes others' information. They link to mechanism design, communication and regulation, and have generated a large theoretical and applied literature.
assessment.attribution: Kamenica and Gentzkow established Bayesian persuasion (2011). Morris, with Bergemann, developed information design and robust predictions across information structures, building on the earlier global-games work. Bergemann is a very strong alternative to Morris or Gentzkow, so the three-name choice is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Core results date from about 2011 and the Bergemann-Morris work from about 2013-2019. Theoretical influence is clear, but long-run empirical validation and policy use are still developing.
uncertainties: The field is relatively young, and the committee may prefer to wait.
Gentzkow's other empirical work (media) could complicate how credit is framed.
Choosing among Bergemann, Morris, Kamenica and Gentzkow is difficult.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Work on trade exposure from China (the 'China shock') and on tasks and technology reshaped how economists think about local labour-market adjustment, polarisation and the distributional costs of trade. It has had major influence on both research and policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the central authors of the China-shock studies. Katz and Autor also did earlier foundational work on skill-biased technological change and tasks, which would favour including Katz or Acemoglu-style task models, so the credit set is contestable.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from 2013-2016, and the field has had a decade of replication, extension and critique. Maturity is moderate to high.
uncertainties: Identification and external validity of the shift-share design have been debated.
The tasks and technology literature has other contributors, and the boundary of the discovery is unclear.
The committee may prefer a broader prize on labour-market inequality.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work combines adverse-selection theory with credible empirical measurement in insurance markets. It quantifies selection and moral hazard, shows that welfare costs depend on the market setting, and informs health-insurance design and regulation.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading empirical figures, and Salanie (with Chiappori) provided the early positive-correlation test and related contributions. Chiappori, who is credited only under B013, is also important for the early tests, so the credit set is somewhat contested. Mixed theory and empirical credit makes the grouping reasonable but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of research with extensive application. The work has influenced policy, though some empirical conclusions remain context-specific.
uncertainties: Findings vary across markets and institutional settings.
The committee may regard the work as applied extensions of information-economics prizes (Akerlof-Spence-Stiglitz).
Chiappori is not among this candidate's credited names, which may blur attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification replaces strong, untestable assumptions with bounds and sets, thereby changing how inference is made under weak assumptions. Manski founded the approach, and Tamer and Molinari developed its inferential and applied implementation.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator, with work from the late 1980s onward. Tamer and Molinari were central to modern inference methods. A Manski-led recognition is plausible, but sharing among later contributors is less clear.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work is decades old, and the methodology has become standard in many applications. Adoption in applied work is uneven.
uncertainties: Practical adoption is narrower than for point-identified methods.
Related moment-inequality contributors outside the credited names (such as Chernozhukov, Hong and Tamer) may raise attribution issues.
I am less certain how the committee values pure methodology against empirical practice.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamic panel GMM estimators (Arellano-Bond, Arellano-Bover, Blundell-Bond) are among the most widely used tools in applied economics, with large practical influence on empirical work in growth, labour, finance and IO.
assessment.attribution: The three names are the standard authors of the estimators. Anderson-Hsiao, Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen, and Hansen's GMM (already honoured) are important predecessors, so part of the credit is shared with earlier work.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of usage, extension and critique, including known weak-instrument and instrument-proliferation concerns. The methods are well established.
uncertainties: The committee might view the contribution as a refinement of GMM rather than a conceptual breakthrough.
Blundell also appears in B029, which could affect how his recognition is weighed.
Known pitfalls in practice, such as too many instruments, may temper enthusiasm.
